title: Chapter 237: Tell Me Your Story
html:
Only three will remain…

A chill passed through Chen Ge’s heart. In this place, being eliminated probably meant death.

“Go over there. You still haven’t earned the right to sit with us,” the fifth person on the right said. He was closest to Chen Ge, and he eyed him with interest. “I like your mask.”

Chen Ge ignored him and walked to stand beside the three new members.

“No. 1, continue your story. No one will interrupt you again.” The first man on the left appeared to be the society’s leader; his word was law.

The newcomer designated No. 1 was elderly. A black mask covered his entire face but left his white hair exposed. His limbs were thin, his body frail, and age spots marked the loose skin of his bare arms.

“Then I shall continue.” No. 1 coughed. He waved his arms habitually while speaking, lending his movements an incongruously comical air.

“This happened at the People’s Hospital. I witnessed it myself, so I know it is true. I have lung cancer and was receiving treatment in the intensive care unit.

“An old man shared the room with me. I don’t know what illness afflicted him, but he suffered terribly, lingering on the boundary between life and death.

“The story began one night a week ago. He was a light sleeper who woke at the slightest sound. That night, I suddenly realized he was awake, staring at a particular spot in the room.

“I looked too, but nothing was there. I switched on the light and asked what he was watching. He said someone was standing in that spot.

“When I asked him to describe the person—their face, their clothing—the old man stammered and could not answer. Around midnight the following night, the room felt unusually cold. I woke to find him lying in the next bed, staring at me with bulging eyes.

“It frightened me half to death. When I turned on the light, he looked away. No matter what I asked, he refused to speak.

“On the third night, I did not dare switch off the bedside lamp. Its dim glow comforted me enough to sleep until morning. But when I awoke, dusty footprints covered my sheets and mattress, as though someone had stood on my bed during the night.

“The sight unhinged me. I felt certain something terrible would happen the moment I slept, so I rested only during the day and forced myself to remain awake at night.

“Nothing happened on the fourth day, but on the night of the fifth day, I saw something scary.

“After midnight, the old man rose from his bed and stood on tiptoe—like this...”

No. 1 let his arms hang at his sides and mimicked the old man, rising onto his toes and hopping around the room. The performance was deeply unsettling.

“He circled my bed several times. I had no idea what he was doing. His cheeks had sunk inward while his eyes protruded, and the wrinkles of his face bunched together. I shouted until he woke. He returned to bed, but his gaze remained fixed on the door.

“He said someone outside was calling his name, but he did not know whether he should answer.

“After nightfall on the sixth day, his condition deteriorated. He could not speak through his endless coughing; it sounded as though something were lodged in his windpipe. The doctors performed an emergency procedure, and his condition finally stabilized after 11 p.m. But his face had turned deathly pale, as if veiled by gray mist.

“After midnight, he opened his eyes again. He stared at the door, mumbling continuously. At one in the morning, he climbed out of bed and shuffled from the room in that strange posture. No one has seen him since.”

When he was done, No. 1 started to cough again. He looked very fragile.

“Fascinating story.” The first man on the left nodded.

“Thank you for the compliment.” No. 1’s laugh sounded like the cawing of a crow; it was grating to the ears.

The people seated along the table began critiquing No. 1’s tale. Chen Ge stood silently at the rear, forming his own judgment. Something had seemed wrong from the old man’s very first sentence.

No. 1 claimed to have shared an intensive-care room, but as far as Chen Ge knew, most ICU rooms in Jiujiang held only one patient.

At first, Chen Ge thought he was lying. But the longer he listened, the more certain he became that No. 1 was telling his own story. He was the dying patient who had left the hospital on tiptoe.

The timeline fit. No. 1’s story had begun a week earlier, and the patient disappeared after midnight on the sixth night. Tonight was the seventh.

The Ghost Stories Society required every account to be true, and no one at the table objected, further suggesting that the old man’s tale was genuine. Lowering his head, Chen Ge glanced sideways at No. 1’s feet. The man appeared to cast no shadow.

“No. 1’s story is very interesting, a good beginning. Now we shall listen to No. 2’s story,” the first man on the left said, and the other people immediately became quiet.

“It’s your turn, No. 2.” No. 1 was weirdly excited, and he kept coughing.

No. 2 wore a foul-smelling jacket and a cheap plastic pig mask of the sort sold at roadside stalls. He was nearly as tall as Chen Ge but extremely thin.

“My ex-wife told me this story, but I guarantee that it is true. She taught dance at a school, and one girl in her class possessed extraordinary talent. In appearance, ability, and physique, she stood far above the others.” No. 2 coughed softly. “The child was a true white swan. Beside her, the other students were no more than ugly ducklings.

“Several years ago, my ex-wife selected six girls from her class to form a troupe for the city dance competition. Consumed by envy, five of them banded together and ostracized the most talented girl.

“She practically carried the troupe to victory, yet no one invited her to the celebration afterward.

“To prepare for the provincial competition, all six trained throughout the summer holiday. That was when the real conflict erupted.”
